Introduction

The structure theorem, stated for finitely generated modules over PIDs, is a nice and elementary example of the usefulness of method of representation (in this case, that of a ring). Many important results in algebra follows immediately from this theorem: the structure theorem of finite abelian groups, rational canonical forms of matrices, also Jordan canonical forms, Cayley-Hamilton theorem. We will discuss the main theorem, with enough preparation until the proof seems trivial (thus omitted and refered to [A]: Artin., Algebra.) Several mentioned consequences will also be discussed. One of the slightly technical result is refered to a different exposition [C]: Conrad., Modules over a PID.

Definition 1 Let R {R}R be a commutative ring with identity. A (left) R {R}R-module M {M}M is an abelian group (+) {(+)}(+) and scalar multiplication R×M→M {R\times M\rightarrow M}R×M→M, (r,m)↦rm {(r,m)\mapsto rm}(r,m)↦rm such that

  1. 1m=m {1m=m}1m=m for all m∈M {m\in M}m∈M;
  2. r(m+n)=rm+rn {r(m+n)=rm+rn}r(m+n)=rm+rn;
  3. (r+s)m=rm+rs {(r+s)m=rm+rs}(r+s)m=rm+rs;
  4. (rs)m=r(sm) {\left(rs\right)m=r\left(sm\right)}(rs)m=r(sm).

Note that the above rules are exactly those for a vector space. A submodule N {N}N of M {M}M is a nonempty subset that is closed under addition and scalar multipilication, hence it inherits the module structure from M {M}M. A map φ:M1→M1 {\varphi:M_{1}\rightarrow M_{1}}φ:M1​→M1​ between two R {R}R-modules is called a R {R}R-module homomorphism if it is R {R}R-linear: φ {\varphi}φ respect the group addition and scalar multiplication.

In the following we will be assuming the ring R {R}R to be a Principal Ideal Domain. Recall that a PID is an integral domain such that all its ideals are principal, i.e. generated by one element from the ring. The nice thing about a PID is that the property that the greatest common divisor of the elements in a set B {B}B can be written as a linear combination the elements in B {B}B. This is a generalization of the property of integers.

As a non-example, we have the notion of greatest common divisor for the UFD K[x,y] {K[x,y]}K[x,y], where K {K}K is a field. The greatest common divisor of x {x}x and y {y}y is clearly 1∈K {1\in K}1∈K, however, the ideal (x,y) {(x,y)}(x,y) generated by x {x}x and y {y}y is not (1)=K {(1)=K}(1)=K, whereas in Z {\mathbb{Z}}Z, or any PID, we would have the two things coincide. On the other hand, in general not every element r∈R {r\in R}r∈R has a multiplicative inverse. This makes the strucutre of a module more complicated than a vector space.

The following theorem will be fundamental in understanding the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over PIDs.

Then there is a canonical R {R}R-module isomorphism φ~:M/ker⁡φ→N {\tilde{\varphi}:M\big/\ker\varphi\rightarrow N}φ~​:M/kerφ→N, mˉ↦φ(m) {\bar{m}\mapsto\varphi(m)}mˉ↦φ(m) where mˉ {\bar{m}}mˉ is the coset m+ker⁡φ {m+\ker\varphi}m+kerφ. Moreover, there is a one-one correspondence between each submodule in N {N}N and each submodule in M {M}M that contains ker⁡φ {\ker\varphi}kerφ.

We check that it respects the module operations. Take mˉ,nˉ∈M/ker⁡φ {\bar{m},\bar{n}\in M\big/\ker\varphi}mˉ,nˉ∈M/kerφ and r∈R {r\in R}r∈R. They can be represented by m {m}m, n {n}n and any other representitives of them will be differed by an element in ker⁡φ {\ker\varphi}kerφ. Now

Moreover, any ideal J⊂N {J\subset N}J⊂N will correspond to some ideal φ−1(J)=φ~−1(J)+ker⁡φ {\varphi^{-1}(J)=\tilde{\varphi}^{-1}(J)+\ker\varphi}φ−1(J)=φ~​−1(J)+kerφ in M {M}M. □ \Box□

The basic example of finitely generated free modules: Rn {R^{n}}Rn

The set Rn=R×⋯×R {R^{n}=R\times\cdots\times R}Rn=R×⋯×R has a natural R {R}R-module structure: the elements are n {n}n-tuples of the elements in the ring R {R}R, and the addtion and scalar multiplication are defined as in the case of vector space. We have an obvous set of generators, namely the finite set

{(1,0,…,0),…,(0,…,1,…,0),…(0,0,…,1)},\displaystyle \{(1,0,\dots,0),\dots,(0,\dots,1,\dots,0),\dots(0,0,\dots,1)\},{(1,0,…,0),…,(0,…,1,…,0),…(0,0,…,1)},

in the sense that taking linear combinations of these will generate Rn {R^{n}}Rn. Moreover, they form a R-linearly independent, hence a basis, corresponding to the notions in linear algebra. In this case we say Rn {R^{n}}Rn is a finitely generated free module. Any finitely generated R {R}R-module with a basis in the above sense, will admit a invaraint basis number, which will be called the rank of the module. And so the R {R}R-module will be isomorphic to some Rn {R^{n}}Rn. In fact, this is true for any commutative ring. Moreover, when R {R}R is a PID, we know everything about its submodules.

Proposition 3 Let M {M}M be a free R {R}R-module. R {R}R is a PID if and only if any submodule of M {M}M is free . In the case M {M}M is finitely generated with rank n {n}n, then any submodule of M {M}M is of rank ≤n {\leq n}≤n.

We need a slightly ajusted version of Theorem 2:

Lemma 4 Let M {M}M, N {N}N be R {R}R-modules and N {N}N is free, and φ:M→N {\varphi:M\rightarrow N}φ:M→N a surjective homomorphism. Then there is a free submodule F {F}F of M {M}M such that φ(F)≅N {\varphi(F)\cong N}φ(F)≅N and

M≅F⊕ker⁡φ.\displaystyle M\cong F\oplus\ker\varphi.M≅F⊕kerφ.

Proof of the proposition: We prove the case that M {M}M is finitely generated. Suppose R {R}R is a PID, and we can take M=Rn {M=R^{n}}M=Rn. We do an induction on n {n}n. When n=1 {n=1}n=1, R {R}R as a R {R}R-module has all its submoudules being its ideals. Since R {R}R is a PID, it is clear that any nonzero ideal I=(a)=aR {I=(a)=aR}I=(a)=aR is generated by an element a∈M\{0} {a\in M\backslash\{0\}}a∈M\{0}. In fact, the map R→aR {R\rightarrow aR}R→aR is a R {R}R-module isomorphism. Now suppose the statement is true for some n≥1 {n\geq1}n≥1. Let M⊂Rn+1 {M\subset R^{n+1}}M⊂Rn+1 be a submodule, and π:Rn+1→Rn {\pi:R^{n+1}\rightarrow R^{n}}π:Rn+1→Rn be the projection of its first n {n}n coordinate. Then π(M)⊂Rn {\pi(M)\subset R^{n}}π(M)⊂Rn is a free submodule of rank ≤n {\leq n}≤n by the induction hypothesis. We restrict the map to π∣M:M→π(M) {\pi\big|_{M}:M\rightarrow\pi(M)}π​M​:M→π(M). Now that π∣M {\pi\big|_{M}}π​M​ is surjective, we have by Lemma 4.

M≅ker⁡π∣M⊕π(M),\displaystyle M\cong\ker\pi\big|_{M}\oplus\pi(M),M≅kerπ​M​⊕π(M),

where ker⁡π∣M=M∩(0n⊕R) {\ker\pi\big|_{M}=M\cap(0^{n}\oplus R)}kerπ​M​=M∩(0n⊕R) and it is easy to see that (0n⊕R) {(0^{n}\oplus R)}(0n⊕R) is a free module of rank 1 {1}1. Thus ker⁡π∣M {\ker\pi\big|_{M}}kerπ​M​ is free with rank ≤1 {\leq1}≤1. Hence M {M}M is free of rank ≤n+1 {\leq n+1}≤n+1. Conversely, suppose any submodule of Rn {R^{n}}Rn is free. Then we have R⊂Rn {R\subset R^{n}}R⊂Rn as a free submodule. To show R {R}R is a PID, note that for a∈R\{0} {a\in R\backslash\{0\}}a∈R\{0}, aR {aR}aR as a submodule of Rn {R^{n}}Rn is free. Hence R {R}R is neccessarily an integral domain. Furthermore, any ideal I⊂R {I\subset R}I⊂R as a submodule of Rn {R^{n}}Rn is free. Since R {R}R is commutative, the basis of R {R}R cannot contain more than two elements. Hence R {R}R is a PID. □ \Box□

Of course, a finitely generated module need not have a basis.

Example 1 Z/nZ {\mathbb{Z}\big/n\mathbb{Z}}Z/nZ where n≥1 {n\geq1}n≥1 as a finitely generated Z {\mathbb{Z}}Z-module does not have a basis. Note that {1ˉ} {\{\bar{1}\}}{1ˉ} is not a basis: n⋅1ˉ=0ˉ {n\cdot\bar{1}=\bar{0}}n⋅1ˉ=0ˉ. This shows that quotients of free modules need not be free. More generally, any finite abelian group as a Z {\mathbb{Z}}Z-module does not have a basis over Z {\mathbb{Z}}Z.

The above example is at the other extreme: they don't have any free submodule.

Definition 5 Let M {M}M be a R {R}R-module. An element m∈M {m\in M}m∈M is called a torsion element if rm=0 {rm=0}rm=0 for some r∈R\{0} {r\in R\backslash\{0\}}r∈R\{0}. M {M}M is called a torsion R {R}R-module if every element is a torsion element. M {M}M is said to be torsion-free if it has no torsion elements.

Proposition 6
The set of all torsion elements in the R {R}R-module M {M}M is a submodule, denoted Etor {E_{tor}}Etor​.

Proof: Recall that R {R}R is an integral domain: if x,y∈Etor {x,y\in E_{tor}}x,y∈Etor​, then sx=0 {sx=0}sx=0 and ty=0 {ty=0}ty=0 for some s,t∈R\{0} {s,t\in R\backslash\{0\}}s,t∈R\{0}. Then since st=ts∈R\{0} {st=ts\in R\backslash\{0\}}st=ts∈R\{0}, we have

st(x+y)=0.\displaystyle st(x+y)=0.st(x+y)=0.

So x+y=Etor {x+y=E_{tor}}x+y=Etor​. Other properties of a submodule are easy to verify. □ \Box□

In general there is a difference between a R {R}R-module being free and being torsion-free. For example, Q {\mathbb{Q}}Q as a Z {\mathbb{Z}}Z-module is torsion-free, but it is not free: it has no basis over Z {\mathbb{Z}}Z. However, if M {M}M is a finitely generated R {R}R-module which is torsion-free, then it is free: there exists an R {R}R-module embedding M↪Rn {M\hookrightarrow R^{n}}M↪Rn, and as a submodule of Rn {R^{n}}Rn, M {M}M will be a free module thanks to Proposition 3. The details of the embedding can be found in [C].

The starting point to understand the structure of a finitely generated module over a PID is the following theorem:

Theorem 7 Let M {M}M be a finitely generated R {R}R-module, where R {R}R is a PID. Then M/Mtor {M\big/M_{tor}}M/Mtor​ is free. There exists a free submodule F {F}F of M {M}M such that M {M}M is a direct sum

M=Mtor⊕F.\displaystyle M=M_{tor}\oplus F.M=Mtor​⊕F.

It is easy to prove that the module M/Mtor {M\big/M_{tor}}M/Mtor​ is torsion-free and finitely generated. Hence it is free. Consider now the projection to the free module M→M/Mtor {M\rightarrow M\big/M_{tor}}M→M/Mtor​. Its kernel is exactly Mtor {M_{tor}}Mtor​. Hence by Lemma 4 there exists a free module F {F}F such that M {M}M is the desired direct sum.
The work now is to understand Mtor {M_{tor}}Mtor​. Thus now we assume M {M}M is a finitely generated torsion R {R}R-module over a PID.

By Theorem 2, M≅Rn/ker⁡φ {M\cong R^{n}\big/\ker\varphi}M≅Rn/kerφ. To understand M {M}M is to understand the quotient Rn/ker⁡φ {R^{n}\big/\ker\varphi}Rn/kerφ. We have

Theorem 8 A submodule M⊂Rn {M\subset R^{n}}M⊂Rn has rank n {n}n if and only if Rn/M {R^{n}\big/M}Rn/M is a torsion module.

Variants of the Structure Theorem

Since elements in a PID admit unique factorization into irreducibles (or equivalently in this case, primes, since in a UFD primes and irreducibles are the same), each R/(di) {R\big/(d_{i})}R/(di​) admits a primary decomposition. This follows from a more general result for commutative rings:
